newsitem.title: UK: London protesters mark "Bloody Sunday" anniversary.
newsitem.headline: London protesters mark "Bloody Sunday" anniversary.

text.p: Hundreds of chanting protesters marched through London on Saturday to demand an apology from the British government for the 1972 "Bloody Sunday" killings in Northern Ireland in which 13 Catholics died.
"It was sheer unadulterated murder," read one placard, referring to January 30, 1972 when British troops opened fire on nationalist demonstrators in the town of Londonderry.
"Until this day the British government has said that those who died deserved to die," said Gerry Duddy, whose 17-year-old brother Jackie was the youngest victim.
"My brother didn't deserve to die...it is time they apologised."

The dead were protesting against British internment of several hundred Catholics opposed to rule from London of Northern Ireland, which has a Protestant majority that generally favours keeping the link with Britain.
A British government inquiry into what quickly became known as "Bloody Sunday" exonerated the troops.
Jeremy Corbyn, a left-wing member of the opposition Labour party, told the crowd that he had submitted a motion to parliament calling for an official apology.
The killings were a defining moment in the conflict over the future of British rule in Northern Ireland, helping to swell the ranks of Irish Republican Army (IRA) guerrillas.

"The people who marched on that day posed a tremendous challenge to the Unionists (Northern Irish Protestants) and the British government," said Martin McGuiness of Sinn Fein, the IRA's political wing.
"Ever since there has been an intractable conflict there."
The protesters marching through north London included a wide mixture of anarchists, young communists, Irish solidarity groups and ordinary Irish and British ciitzens.
"It was just another piece of evidence of how the British treat the Irish," said Peter White, a retired gardener who travelled from western England to attend the rally.
"I don't think they will ever apologise," said the bearded 67-year-old, sporting a solidarity ribbon.
